prompt: Review this anchor as its assigned subagent. Enumerate ALL requirements, qualifications, edge cases and scenarios. Inspect all supplied implementation and test fragments and trace each aspect to implementation behavior and actual test assertions or justified TODO/N/A evidence. Passing tests and associations alone are insufficient. Follow helpers and capture every additional source dependency with cargo meta review read ANCHOR PATH [selector] before completing the report. Explain prerequisites for justified TODO tests; do not claim deferred behavior is implemented. Distinguish source inspection from commands actually executed. Write a JSON report containing reviewer, report, and requested_edits. Leave requested_edits empty only when every aspect is accounted for and no edits are needed. Otherwise list concrete changes, including missing tests or justified TODO tests with prerequisite comments. Run cargo meta review record ANCHOR REPORT_FILE to finish. After edits or stale-input rejection, run cargo meta review start ANCHOR and review the fresh inputs. The gate fails until a current report with no requested edits is recorded. Dependency capture is agent-declared.
coordinator_instructions:
Review only your assigned anchor using the sage-review-checklist skill and its start/read/record workflow. Capture these instructions with start --instructions /tmp/anchor-review-instructions.txt. Use captured source context; do not import old approvals or uncaptured coordinator conclusions. Write only your anchor's validations directory and a unique report file under /tmp. Coordinate production, test, and association edits with the coordinator before making them because concurrent reviewers may capture the same files. Capture essential dependencies using review read; report any necessary association additions for coordinated handling. Existing TODO/N/A evidence must be individually justified and remain deferred; do not claim passing placeholders verify functionality. Distinguish source review from tests actually run. On a suspected behavioral violation, coordinate a regression test and follow the skill rather than rubber-stamping. Return a concise summary of the recorded outcome or precise unresolved finding. Do not commit or change unrelated files.

Coordinator authorization: resolve missing evidence as part of this assignment. You may add essential anchor association comments and focused tests (or associate existing substantive tests), then format, run relevant tests, and perform a fresh review. Announce the files you will edit and coordinate with another active reviewer if sharing a file. Do not stop merely to request these routine evidence edits. Production behavioral changes still require reporting a reproduced failure and coordinating the correction with root. Root will perform centralized delegated post-codegen and Sage sanity checks covering all reviewer edits; report your changed paths for that pass. Preserve honest existing TODOs. If an additional implementation obligation is genuinely absent, report it to root rather than disguising the gap as a test TODO.

contents: **External metadata supplies owned facts, never Sage decisions.** The provider may state facts authored by a reachable dependency or the compiler, but it cannot resolve local syntax, select a Sage candidate, prove a Sage goal, normalize an alias, or type-check a Sage body. This is the typed metadata boundary established by [External providers supply facts, not Sage semantic answers](../../../rfds/architectural-foundations/README.md#external-providers-supply-facts-not-sage-semantic-answers).

# Reviewing Specification Implementations and Tests
A validation records an agent's assessment of one specification anchor against
its implementation and tests. The saved context lets `cargo meta` check whether
that assessment still applies. Running tests remains a separate obligation.
## Intended workflow
The main agent discovers review work through a failing `cargo meta check` or
the shared Cargo validation test. Diagnostics identify the affected anchors,
explain why they need review, and direct the agent to the review skill. The
skill delegates one subagent per anchor, supplying its ID and an initial prompt.
The subagent obtains its source context through the review commands, so that
the saved inputs are the same inputs it consumes.
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
participant Main as Main agent
participant Check as Check / Cargo validation test
participant Reviewer as Review subagent (one per anchor)
participant CLI as cargo meta review
participant Files as validations/anchor-id/
Main->>Check: Check current validations
Check-->>Main: Fail: affected anchors, reasons, review skill
Main->>Reviewer: Follow skill, review anchor using initial prompt
Reviewer->>CLI: start anchor
CLI->>Files: Clear old validation, save summary and initial inputs
Note over Check,Files: No output exists: the gate must fail
CLI-->>Reviewer: Print the saved inputs and verification prompt
loop Additional context needed
Reviewer->>CLI: read anchor path selector
CLI->>Files: Append the selected source fragment
CLI-->>Reviewer: Return the exact saved contents
end
Reviewer->>CLI: record anchor report-file
CLI->>Files: Load captured inputs
CLI->>CLI: Verify freshness and report format
alt Inputs changed or report invalid
CLI-->>Reviewer: Reject recording, gate still fails
else Valid submission
CLI->>Files: Save output and recording time, preserve inputs
CLI-->>Reviewer: Report recorded
end
Reviewer-->>Main: Report results and any requested edits
Main->>Check: Check all validations again
alt Every anchor has a current report with no requested edits
Check-->>Main: Pass
else Missing, unfinished, stale, or changes requested
Check-->>Main: Fail with reasons
Note over Main,Reviewer: Resolve edits and repeat review for affected anchors
end
The subagent captures inputs and records its report in the validation directory
created by `start`. Starting a review removes its previous output even when the
source has not changed, so an interrupted review cannot reuse an old approval.
Each additional read is saved before its contents are returned. Recording
checks the captured inputs for freshness and preserves them exactly.
A successful `record` is necessary but does not by itself make the gate pass.
The report must request no edits, its inputs must still be current, and every
other anchor must also satisfy the gate. If edits are requested, the main agent
coordinates them and starts fresh reviews for affected anchors. An accepted
review of justified TODO/N/A evidence leaves that status visible; it does not
claim the deferred behavior is implemented.
The contracts below define the files, selectors, and commands in detail. In
particular, {spec}`meta.reviews.record_required` states the failing-until-recorded
invariant, and {spec}`meta.reviews.review_delegation` defines subagent ownership.
## Validation directory
{anchor}`validation_layout`
Each anchor has one directory named by its complete dotted ID, for example:
```text
validations/meta.reviews.gate/
summary.json
input.json
output.json
`summary.json` identifies the review; `input.json` contains the context captured
for it; `output.json` contains the completed assessment. `cargo meta review start`
creates or resets the directory and writes the first two files. Until recording
completes, `output.json` is absent and the validation cannot satisfy the gate.
The directory name must be a valid anchor ID and match `summary.json`. Starting
a new review discards the previous validation; earlier validations are not
retained.
## `summary.json`: identity and record metadata
{anchor}`summary_format`
The summary contains these fields:
| Field | Meaning |
| `anchor` | Complete dotted ID of the anchor being validated. |
| `started_at_unix_seconds` | Time the review was started, in seconds since the Unix epoch. |
| `recorded_at_unix_seconds` | Time the completed report was recorded; null until recording completes. |
| `schema_version` | Version of the persisted record format. |
| `policy_version` | Version of the rules governing review acceptance. |
Freshness is determined by comparing the recorded inputs with current source,
as defined by
{spec}`meta.reviews.fragment_freshness`.
## `input.json`: the context being reviewed
{anchor}`input_format`
The input contains these fields:
| Field | Meaning |
| `prompt` | Exact verification prompt. |
| `coordinator_instructions` | Additional instructions supplied to the reviewer, in order. |
| `fragments` | Uniform collection of source fragments, including the claim, tests, implementation context, and additional reads. |
| `implementations` | Complete implementation association metadata. |
| `tests` | Complete associated test metadata. |
The following anchors define each part. Source text belongs in the uniform
fragment collection; association metadata identifies the evidence and its
declared status. The collection contains both initial context and later reads.
### Instructions and complete context
{anchor}`review_instructions`
Review inputs preserve the exact verification prompt and any additional
coordinator instructions supplied to the reviewer. These instructions are part
of the recorded context even when they do not originate in a source file.
{anchor}`input_fragments`
Every piece of source context supplied to or consulted by a validation agent is
recorded in one uniform collection of input fragments, whether prepared
automatically, supplied by a coordinator, or declared by the reviewer. Helpers
and surrounding context used during review are additional fragments; recording
only the initial claim and tests does not excuse omitting other context used.
Automatic preparation and recorded reads use the same fragment representation
and freshness checks. Reviewers are responsible for declaring every source
dependency used in their assessment.
### Fragment representation
{anchor}`fragment_format`
Each fragment records its workspace-relative source path, selector, and exact
selected contents. Contents are stored as source lines; joining them with
newline characters recovers the selected text, including its whitespace and
line endings.
The data model is defined below in Rust notation, without prescribing a JSON
encoding:
```rust,ignore
struct InputFragment {
path: String,           // Workspace-relative UTF-8 source file path.
selector: Selector,
contents: Vec<String>, // Join with '\n' to recover the selected text.
enum Selector {
WholeFile,
LineRange { start: usize, end: usize },
Claim { anchor_id: String },
Test {
crate_name: String,
target: String,
rust_path: String,
{anchor}`source_representation`
Claim, implementation, and annotated test source snapshots are stored in `input.json` as
arrays of source lines. Joining an array with newline characters recovers the
snapshot's text, including internal blank lines, whitespace, and markup.
### Selectors
{anchor}`selector_whole_file`
`Selector::WholeFile` selects all contents of the fragment's source file,
including any trailing newline. It carries no additional selector data.
{anchor}`selector_line_range`
`Selector::LineRange { start, end }` selects a one-based, inclusive range of
lines within the fragment's source file. Lines are delimited by `\n`; selected
text retains the original line endings, including the last selected line's
ending if present. Zero, reversed, or out-of-bounds ranges are invalid.
The saved line numbers are used again when checking freshness, so shifting
content across those boundaries may conservatively make the fragment stale.
{anchor}`selector_claim`
`Selector::Claim { anchor_id }` selects the complete claim identified by its
full dotted anchor ID within the fragment's source file, using the shared
anchor-content boundaries and claim-text normalization. The containing document
need not be included. The selector stores no line numbers or byte offsets;
inserting unrelated lines before an unchanged claim does not make the fragment
stale.
{anchor}`selector_test`
`Selector::Test { crate_name, target, rust_path }` selects the complete annotated
Rust test function within the fragment's source file, including attributes,
signature, body, and comments. `crate_name` identifies the Cargo package;
`target` uses the correspondence target identity, including kind and name
(for example `lib:sage_meta` or `test:review`); `rust_path` identifies the fully
qualified function within that target. Identically named functions in different
targets are distinct. The containing file need not be included. The selector
stores no line numbers or byte offsets; inserting unrelated lines before an
unchanged test does not make the fragment stale.
### Claim and evidence metadata
{anchor}`claim_text`
An anchor's review text is the complete source content selected by the
[anchor-content boundaries](anchors.md#anchor-content), with surrounding
whitespace removed. For `.sage` prose, its enclosing common indentation is
removed first; remaining internal whitespace and Markdown markup are preserved.
The saved input covers the same content that the generated anchor views
present as the claim, including any paragraphs, lists, or examples within its
extent.
{anchor}`test_source`
Each associated test's review input contains the complete annotated Rust
function source, including its attributes, signature, body, and contained
comments. It also records the Cargo crate and target, Rust path, file path,
inherited configuration conditions, and ordinary, `todo`, or `not_applicable`
status. Source line numbers and byte offsets are excluded from the input.
{anchor}`complete_test_set`
One review covers one anchor's claim and its complete set of associated tests.
The input records every eligible test associated with that anchor in a
deterministic order. Several tests may cover different parts of a claim; each
test need not establish the whole claim independently.
{anchor}`review_scope`
One review judges both implementation completeness and test adequacy against
an anchor's complete claim. Its saved input includes every implementation
association's crate, target, module, file, cfg conditions, excerpt, region flag,
placeholder status, and explanation, in deterministic order. Source line
numbers and byte offsets are not association metadata. Source context used to
assess these associations is recorded under {spec}`meta.reviews.input_fragments`.
A point marker's five-line preview is navigation context, not a sufficient
boundary for reviewing behavior that depends on other code.
Reviewers follow relevant helpers and dependencies and record the source
fragments they use. They add implementation associations for essential code in
other files before approval. Reviews are source judgments, not proofs; test
execution remains separate evidence.
## `output.json`: the reviewer’s assessment
{anchor}`output_format`
The output contains only the reviewer, report, and requested edits:
```rust,ignore
struct ValidationOutput {
reviewer: String,
report: String,
requested_edits: Vec<String>,

## Freshness and acceptance
{anchor}`fragment_freshness`
Recording and checking resolve every fragment's selector against current source
and compare the selected text with the saved text using exact string equality.
A missing or ambiguous selection, invalid selector, or changed selected text
makes the validation stale or invalid. No selector kind or input origin bypasses
these checks.
{anchor}`fragment_associations`
The complete association set and its metadata remain checked separately from
fragment contents. Adding, removing, or changing an association invalidates the
review even when all saved fragments still resolve to unchanged text.

version, complete claim, and implementation and test inputs match the current
inventory. Source context must satisfy {spec}`meta.reviews.fragment_freshness`
and associations must satisfy {spec}`meta.reviews.fragment_associations`.
Unchanged claims and tests remain reusable when unrelated edits move them, as
specified by their selectors. Changed text within a whole-file fragment,
including blank-line changes, invalidates that fragment. A reusable review must
also have a complete output under {spec}`meta.reviews.output_format` and no
requested edits under {spec}`meta.reviews.decisions`.

### `cargo meta review start <anchor>`

Starting a review validates the requested anchor against the current inventory,
then clears any existing validation for that anchor and sets up
`validations/<anchor>/`. It writes `summary.json` and the initial `input.json`
before printing the exact captured inputs and verification prompt for the agent
to consume. The initial inputs include the complete claim, associated tests,
implementation context, and association metadata defined by
{spec}`meta.reviews.input_format`. Additional coordinator instructions supplied
to the reviewer are captured under {spec}`meta.reviews.review_instructions`.
Starting removes the previous output. After a successful start, the validation
directory must be in a state
that makes `cargo meta check` and the shared Cargo validation test fail for that
anchor, even if its previous validation passed and its source is unchanged.
An interrupted or abandoned review therefore cannot fall back to an
older approval. Unknown or invalid anchor IDs are rejected before clearing any
record. Other anchors' directories are unchanged. A failed start cannot leave
an older output appearing to validate newly captured inputs.

The recorded-read command takes an anchor with an active review directory, a
workspace-relative source path, and a selector from

selects the whole file. It appends the selected contents and selector directly
to that anchor's `input.json` before returning those same contents to the
reviewer. Repeated reads are retained in order. Reads outside the workspace,
invalid selections, and reads without an active unfinished review are rejected.
These fragments participate in the same freshness checks as the initial inputs.
Reviewers declare every additional source dependency through this command and
are responsible for the completeness of those declarations.

metadata. Missing or stale inputs, an unknown anchor, an invalid report, or an

text for the inputs the agent actually reviewed.
On success, recording writes `output.json` and updates the summary's recording

For every anchor requiring re-evaluation, `cargo meta check` and the shared

An interrupted, abandoned, or failed review remains failing; an older report
cannot stand in for the unfinished review.
Recording is necessary but not sufficient: the recorded report must be complete,
request no edits, and still match current inputs. Recording a report that

given the anchor ID and an initial prompt directing it to run

Reviewers trace every requirement to implementation code, checking missing
cases and contradictory behavior. They consider the complete associated test
set and explain which assertions exercise which parts of the claim. They identify a plausible
violation and whether those assertions would detect it.
The scenario, expected outcome, and assertion should be clear from the body of
the test function itself. Parsing, fixture construction, and setup helpers are
reasonable. A call such as `verify_everything()` that hides the meaningful
assertions is insufficient evidence: request a clearer test body instead of
approving it from its name or annotation. Reviewers may read helpers to
understand the test, and capture additional helper fragments through the recorded-read command.
A helper edit outside the supplied files and captured reads does not invalidate a saved review. Running the tests can detect
behavioral changes, but the cached review covers only the snapshotted source.
Add implementation associations to include additional essential source files.
When reviewers suspect a bug, they add an anchor-associated regression test
that exercises the intended behavior and run it against the implementation.
A reproduced behavioral failure yields concrete requested edits, with the test,
command, and observed failure in the report. Do not treat a build or environment
failure as reproduction. If a test cannot reproduce the concern, or a reviewer
cannot work out how to write one, consult the user with the concern and attempts;
leave the affected review unresolved until the concern is resolved. New tests
or associations require starting a fresh review before recording a report.

# Overview
Sage is a demand-driven Rust semantic frontend. Symbols give definitions stable
identities. Parsing and expansion create those symbols; resolution discovers
them; signature and body queries compute semantic products when requested.
Checking a body brings together name resolution, type inference, trait solving,
and elaboration into a completed typed tree.
```mermaid
flowchart LR
Source[Source] --> Symbols[Parse and expand symbols]
Symbols --> Resolve[Resolve names]
Resolve --> Signature[Check signatures]
Signature --> Body[Check and elaborate a body]
Metadata[Dependency metadata] --> Resolve
Metadata --> Signature
Infer[Inference and trait solving] --> Body
Body --> Typed[Typed IR]
This is a map of demand boundaries, not a mandatory batch sequence. Start with
[Crates](crates/README.md) to follow the modeled entities and operations.
- [Meta](meta/README.md) specifies how this book, its architecture language,
source correspondence, and review system work.
- [Tenets](tenets.md) explains the principles behind the design.
- [Anchors](anchor/README.md) lists the specification's named claims with
generated implementation and test status. Every rule has a page connecting
its source definition, implementation excerpts, tests, and review.
- [Crates](crates/README.md) is a guided entry into the compiler model. Its
subchapters render `.sage` declarations and their Rust implementations.
- [RFDs](../rfds/README.md) record changes, alternatives, rationale, and plans.
Their normative changes are expressed directly in this specification.
Markdown and `.sage` are equally authoritative specification formats. Each
anchor states one independently testable claim. A source badge opens the
anchor's generated page; its context link returns to the definition.
**TODO** and **N/A** describe explicit implementation or test entries, not
successful verification. Evidence and status are generated from code, tests,
and saved reviews rather than maintained as a second specification.
For tool usage, start with the [User's Guide](../guide/README.md).

# Architectural Foundations
**Status: Retrospective record.** This record gathers the reasoning behind
foundational choices made while building Sage. It is not a new proposal or a
second specification. Current requirements live in the [Design
specification](../../design/README.md); its anchors and modeled entities carry
implementation and test associations.
The individual sections retain the reasoning and point to the affected
subsystems and more focused RFDs. This record preserves context where no
single original RFD captured the cross-cutting choice.
## Salsa for incremental computation
We use [salsa](https://github.com/salsa-rs/salsa) as the incremental computation
framework for stable semantic demand boundaries. Source and configuration enter
through Salsa inputs; definitions have tracked or interned identity as
appropriate; and reusable semantic products are tracked functions keyed at the
granularity consumers request.
Temporary inference state, speculative candidates, partially checked
expressions, and formatting helpers are not promoted to tracked queries merely
because they perform substantial work. They remain inside the semantic query
which owns their transaction and publishes their completed result. Stash for type-level interning covers
the separate Stash representation used for type and IR storage.
## Stash for type-level interning
Types, CST, and other tree-shaped IR nodes are allocated in an owning `Stash`
(a custom arena with hash-consing) rather than making every node a Salsa
identity. A `Stashed<T>` query result owns its stash and root as one semantic
value; checking reads source stashes and constructs output in a fresh stash.
Solver proof contexts likewise own the stashes in which their temporary values
are meaningful.
This gives Sage compact handles (`Ptr<T>` and `Slice<T>`) with zero-copy
decomposition inside their owning stash, deterministic rooted fingerprints for
Salsa backdating, and an explicit structural-copy boundary between owners. In
release builds a handle is the four-byte entry index. Debug builds add a
four-byte stash identity, making the handle eight bytes and allowing indexing
to diagnose cross-stash use. Release builds rely on the ownership invariant and
the explicit structural-copy APIs: a handle never acquires database-global
meaning and must not be interpreted by another stash merely because its
numeric index matches.
Intern lookup partitions candidates by type, element count, and content hash
before comparing values. Count is a memory-safety boundary: a scalar hash can
collide with an empty slice hash, but lookup must never read that empty entry
as a scalar.
A stash grows by allocating new hash-consed entries, but an allocated entry is
immutable. Transient algorithms such as inference keep mutation in separate
state. When their result is ready to cross a semantic query boundary, they
resolve and structurally copy it into a fresh stash rather than rewriting
arena entries in place. This preserves the content-addressed meaning of every
handle and makes a completed stash an acyclic value graph by construction.
## Tree-sitter for parsing
We use tree-sitter-rust for parsing rather than writing a hand-rolled parser.
It supplies the Rust grammar and error-recovering concrete tree without Sage
duplicating grammar maintenance. Sage immediately lowers the required syntax
into per-item, stash-owned CST; tree-sitter nodes and their identities do not
cross the parse query boundary.
Tree-sitter can support incremental reparsing, but Sage's semantic incremental
contract is expressed through module inputs, stable item symbols, per-item CST
content, and Salsa backdating. This decision does not require downstream phases
to observe or depend upon tree-sitter's internal node reuse.
## Oracle test harness
End-to-end correctness is validated by an "oracle" harness that compiles test programs
with both Sage and rustc. Each side independently emits the same shared,
deterministically serialized reference IR. The conformance decision is exact
textual identity of those outputs.
The per-side adapters perform only representation changes required to reach
the shared schema. The comparator does not normalize a pair of outputs, erase
known differences, reorder values, strip bodies, or otherwise attempt semantic
equivalence. Validation may reject incomplete output before comparison, and a
diagnostic diff may explain an exact mismatch afterward, but neither changes
the equality rule. Stable external identity includes the actual definition kind
of every path segment; an adapter may not reconstruct ancestor kinds from the
leaf kind or from namespace alone. The detailed contract is [Oracle Test
Harness](../../design/crates/sage_oracle_harness/oracle-guide.md#thin-adapters-and-exact-comparison).
## Symbols form the uniform semantic identity family
Top-level and associated definitions represented as symbols—functions, types,
impls, modules, constants, enum variants and constructors, and so on—use
kind-specific local or external identities. Erased `Symbol` values permit
heterogeneous ownership and membership, while wrappers such as `FnSymbol` and
`TraitSymbol` recover the static kind required by semantic operations.
Not every semantic identity is an erased `Symbol`. Generic parameters use the
separate `GenericParam` identity family; fields are identified by owner and
index; locals have body-local IDs. Those representations are deliberately
scoped to the structure which owns them and are not converted to `Symbol`
merely for surface uniformity.
Uniformity therefore applies to definitions in the symbol family and their
conversions, not to every identity-bearing IR node, one storage representation,
or one untyped query surface. Kind-specific tracked structs and methods are
intentional: they expose the fields and operations valid for that definition
kind while types and Typed IR refer to each entity through its appropriate
typed identity.
## Versioned egraph children are inference transactions
Operations that may partially constrain inference state run in a child egraph
version. On complete success, a short-lived probe may collapse its child into
the direct parent; on failure, it discards the child, so partial equalities,
bounds, and wake effects cannot escape. The probe API permits collapse only
when the probe is the parent's only live child, so no sibling can observe its
parent changing underneath an in-progress computation.
Concurrent alternatives are different: each candidate owns an isolated proof
context and performs its speculative matching in a child version of that
context. Candidate versions are never merged into a requester. Each candidate
extracts a canonical response before its isolated context is dropped, so no
alternative-specific choice can become another candidate's ancestor state.
Because descendants read sparse state through their ancestry, per-version
writes target leaf versions only. Creating a child freezes its parent until
every child is discarded or the sole child is atomically collapsed; read-only
lookup from the frozen parent is allowed, but path compression, variable
allocation, equality/bound changes, rebuild publication, semantic revisions,
and wake publication are not. Append-only allocation in the proof context's
shared `Stash` is the sole non-version fact exempt from this rule. This gives
each branch a stable ancestor snapshot without copying the parent maps.
## Inference-variable identities are unique across egraph versions
An `InferVarIndex` identifies one inference variable throughout an egraph; two
sibling versions never reuse the same index for different variables. Metadata
records the version which owns each variable, and an explicit-version egraph
operation may access it only from that version or a descendant. Version handles
are not reused without a generation, so a discarded variable's recorded owner
cannot become valid again accidentally.
This uses more stash entries than branch-relative index reuse, but prevents a
`Ty::InferVar` allocated in one concurrent candidate from being reinterpreted
as a sibling's variable. It also makes response extraction, cancellation, and
exclusive child-to-parent commits enforceable at the type-identity boundary.
Variable metadata keeps immutable creation universe separate from a versioned
current universe ceiling. Equality may transactionally lower that ceiling to
prevent delayed leaks through nested flexible variables; committed lowering is
a semantic wake/revision, and canonical query identity uses the current ceiling.
## Whiteboard producers own isolated proof contexts
Every in-progress trait-solver frame imports its canonical query into a fresh
proof stash and egraph owned by the frame producer. Candidate alternatives do
the same before opening their local child transaction. The per-query
whiteboard, rather than a shared egraph root, is the common coordination point:
it owns producer futures, subscriptions, parent links, and branch-independent
stashed responses.
This costs additional per-frame instantiation, but it prevents a suspended
producer from borrowing a shared mutable egraph and makes requester
cancellation independent from producer lifetime. Raw inference-variable and
version identities cannot cross contexts because every published response is
validated and canonicalized first.
## Trait solving is groundness-sensitive and resource-bounded
A canonical trait query is ground when it has no flexible existential inputs;
rigid generic placeholders still count as ground. Non-ground queries must
terminate and publish only sound proofs, substitutions, hard hints, and
negative results, but they may return ambiguity despite a valid answer. Ground
queries are sound and complete unless an explicit deterministic resource limit
is exceeded.
Ambiguity and resource exhaustion are distinct results. Depth, canonical term
size, logical work, and fixpoint limits never become logical `No`. For fixed
canonical inputs and configured limits, polling order may change discovery and
resource use but not the final canonical solver response. Sage therefore aims
for broad rustc compatibility without requiring exactly the same source type
annotations in every non-ground inference case.
The detailed contract lives in [Trait Solver Design](../../design/crates/sage_ir/solver-guide.md).
This soundness contract is modulo the explicit temporary lifetime and borrow
checking omission in Lifetimes collapse to `Dummy` and borrow checking is deferred. Type-only and trait-selection uncertainty must still
be represented soundly; Lifetimes collapse to `Dummy` and borrow checking is deferred does not permit a non-lifetime ambiguity to be
guessed.
## Trait impl discovery is global and trait-keyed
Trait candidate discovery covers every impl visible in the current compilation
through local source and reachable external-crate metadata. The fixed trait is
the mandatory primary query key; the solver does not enumerate impls for every
trait and filter them only during proof execution.
A simplified self-type key may refine lookup when its rigid outer shape is
known. Such an index is conservative: it may return extra candidates but never
omit an applicable specific, blanket, or unclassifiable impl. Indexed and
exhaustive discovery have identical solver meaning. The trait key, and
eventually compatible self-type partitions, also form the semantic lookup
boundary.
The local incremental firewall has two layers. A crate-owned tracked index has
stable identity and a private tracked map containing deterministic trait
buckets plus explicit completeness hazards. Keyed tracked lookup methods are
the only readers of that map. An unrelated impl edit may rebuild the index and
reexecute a cheap lookup for another trait; when that lookup returns the same
bucket, Salsa backdates it. The edit must not propagate into unrelated impl
signature lowering, solver evaluation, normalization, or body checking.
Unknown expansion which could emit an impl for any trait is a global hazard and
legitimately affects every lookup.
The current `local_impl_candidates(LocalCrateSymbol, TraitSymbol)` query is a
trait-keyed local source backed by a provisional linear module-tree scan. It
resolves each impl's trait identity first and lowers a full header only for the
requested trait. Its result carries conservative expansion/header completeness,
and it excludes impls with unrepresented active attribute transformations from
definite candidates. Exact orphan-rule pruning also skips local discovery for
a foreign trait with no trait arguments on a non-fundamental foreign nominal
self type. Because the backing identity scan still depends on the expanded
module tree, the destination incremental firewall is not yet built: an
unrelated trait impl edit can propagate through the current candidate query
despite producing the same candidates.
Reachable external-crate coverage and conservative external self-head
partitioning are built; trait-partitioned local source dependencies and their
edit-invalidation matrix remain outstanding. The destination and required
conformance tests live in
[Trait Solver Design](../../design/crates/sage_ir/solver-guide.md) and the
[Trait Impl Candidate Discovery RFD](../trait-impl-candidate-discovery/README.md).
## Completed bodies are elaborated typed trees
`LocalFnSym::body` returns a fully typed, fully resolved, tree-structured IR.
Implicit type-directed operations such as receiver dereference, autoref,
coercion, and unsizing are materialized as nodes. Method syntax, unresolved
field names, inference variables, and adjustment lists do not survive in a
successful completed body.
Structured control flow, closures, and async bodies remain above MIR: the IR
does not introduce basic blocks, drop schedules, or coroutine state-machine
layout. Candidate selection may use source-shaped nodes and adjustment recipes
internally, but those are consumed inside the body query. The full destination
contract is [Typed IR](../../design/crates/sage_ir/typed-ir-guide.md).
## Lifetimes collapse to `Dummy` and borrow checking is deferred
Every explicit, elided, universal, existential, imported, and synthesized
lifetime immediately becomes `Lifetime::Dummy` during checking. Sage does not
create lifetime inference variables. `Outlives(Dummy, Dummy)` is true, and
lifetime relationships cannot reject a program.
Borrow and dereference operations remain explicit in typed IR because they
affect ordinary types and calls, but their validity is not checked. This is a
known temporary soundness hole. A dedicated variant is used instead of
`'static` or post-analysis erasure so the omission is visible and its eventual
removal is mechanically enforced. A future unified type-and-lifetime
inference design supersedes this decision.
## Named, associated, and opaque aliases share one semantic family
The type representation distinguishes rigid types from alias types. Rigid
constructors such as `Vec` are structural and do not normalize. `AliasTy` has
three semantic variants: `Named` for a user-defined type alias, `Associated`
for an associated-type projection, and `Opaque` for an opaque type. Every
alias retains its definition identity and generic arguments.
Normalization is a semantic operation, not an eager erasure pass. Named aliases
reveal their substituted right-hand sides infallibly. Associated types normalize
through trait matching. Opaques reveal only within their definition boundary
or in a future code-generation mode. The typing/reveal context is consequently
part of the normalization query's semantic input. Solver operations return goal-specific semantic outputs specifies how that
operation returns its result.
An unrevealed alias is not devoid of facts. Bounds declared on associated and
opaque types may prove predicates without normalization, and identical alias
applications may be related structurally. The complete destination contract
is split between [Typed IR](../../design/crates/sage_ir/typed-ir-guide.md#rigid-and-alias-types) and [Trait
Solver Design](../../design/crates/sage_ir/solver-guide.md#alias-types-and-normalization).
## Solver operations return goal-specific semantic outputs
The solver distinguishes value-producing operations from the proposition
language used for assumptions and residual conditions. A proof operation
returns `GoalOutput::Proven`; normalization takes only an alias as input and
returns `GoalOutput::Type`. A successful response carries that output alongside
its substitution and residual proof goal.
Normalization is therefore modeled as `Normalize(alias) -> Type`, not as the
predicate `NormalizesTo(alias, caller_output)` and not as a convention where a
fresh output inference variable must be recovered from the response
substitution. The caller relates the returned type to any expected type only
after candidate answers have been merged, so its expectation cannot select an
otherwise ambiguous candidate.
The output is part of the canonical response: its response-local variables are
bound, copied, occurs-checked, universe-checked, cached, compared, and merged.
An unconditional `Proven` answer can absorb sibling proofs, but an unconditional
type result cannot absorb a sibling which may return a different type unless
candidate priority or output equivalence justifies it.
`GoalOutput` is extensible for future non-type operations such as callable
instance resolution or vtable construction. Those representations remain
unsettled; this decision only prevents them from being forced through the type
variant. Trait implementation proof continues to return `Proven`, never a
selected impl identity. See [Trait Solver Design](../../design/crates/sage_ir/solver-guide.md#knowledge-returned-by-the-solver)
and the [Associated Type Normalization RFD](../associated-type-normalization/README.md).
## Cross-item dependencies stop at semantic interfaces
A definition's symbol is the stable key for its semantic products. Its checked
signature is the primary interface other definitions consume; field, member,
and other language-required interfaces may be separate narrow keyed products.
Its body and checking temporaries are not interfaces. A caller may read the
callee's signature and relevant trait or metadata facts, but never the callee
body. Signature checking likewise does not eagerly check the definition's
body.
This boundary applies to dependency meaning even when a provisional coarse
input causes extra execution. If reexecution produces an equal public semantic
value, Salsa backdating stops propagation before unrelated downstream
consumers. Narrower future inputs should reduce that extra execution without
changing the semantic boundary.
This choice lets Sage type-check one body without checking the crate eagerly,
makes interface-preserving edits reusable, and gives query-trace tests a clear
set of forbidden dependencies. Its chapter-level consequences are

[crates.sage_ir.crate.narrow_demands](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/crate/narrow_demands.html), [crates.sage_ir.symbols.body_interfaces](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/symbols/body_interfaces.html), and
[crates.sage_ir.crate.reexecution_and_invalidation](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/crate/reexecution_and_invalidation.html).
## Incompleteness is an explicit terminal outcome
A phase or semantic subsystem distinguishes a complete result from a
conservative result limited by invalid or ambiguous source, unsupported Sage
functionality, unavailable external facts, or an explicit resource bound.
Such incompleteness is terminal for the current inputs and limits: continuing
to poll or schedule the same computation is not expected to make it complete.
An incomplete result may retain partial information for diagnostics or
conservative recovery, but it must identify which completeness guarantee is
absent and must not be presented as a successful complete value. Resource
exhaustion and ambiguity also remain distinct from a logical negative answer.
Repeating the operation may produce a different outcome only after an input,
environment, or configured limit changes.
This decision separates semantic recovery from asynchronous progress and
prevents downstream consumers from treating missing work as negative
evidence. The pipeline-wide consequence and verification contract is
[crates.sage_ir.crate.terminal_incompleteness](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/crate/terminal_incompleteness.html); solver-specific resource and groundness
semantics remain in [Trait solving is groundness-sensitive and resource-bounded](#trait-solving-is-groundness-sensitive-and-resource-bounded).
## Nested spans are relative to stable item provenance
Each source-root item carries an absolute range in a `ParseSource`. A nested
definition carries its placement relative to its immediate owner, and syntax
or Typed IR inside any represented item carries byte ranges relative to that
item's own start. Resolving a nested range composes the owner chain to the
source root and preserves the same parse-source identity. For example, an
associated method is relative to its trait or impl, while the method's body is
relative to the method. Generated parse sources use stable occurrence identity
while their generated text and current origin coordinates remain tracked facts.
This split keeps position lookup and diagnostics accurate while preventing an
offset-only edit before an otherwise unchanged item, including an edit to an
earlier sibling associated item, from changing every span inside its semantic
content. Queries which need source positions may observe the composed absolute
span; ordinary signature and body semantics should depend on the relative
content instead.
The representation and edit-verification requirements are

[crates.sage_ir.types.spans.relative_composition](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/types/spans/relative_composition.html), [crates.sage_ir.types.spans.generated_identity](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/types/spans/generated_identity.html), and
[crates.sage_ir.types.spans.offset_reuse](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/types/spans/offset_reuse.html). The historical rationale is recorded in the
[Relative Span Model RFD](../relative-span-model/README.md).
## External providers supply facts, not Sage semantic answers
Rustc-backed providers may authoritatively expose facts owned by reachable
dependency crates and the compilation environment: definition identity,
ownership, signatures, predicates, associated items and values, impl headers,
and other exported metadata. Sage lowers those facts into its own symbol,
type, stash, and query representations at narrow keyed boundaries.
The provider does not resolve Sage-local source, select a method or impl for a
Sage body, prove a Sage trait goal, normalize an alias on Sage's behalf, or
produce Sage's checked body. Those operations remain in Sage even when their
inputs include authoritative external facts. Likewise, the rustc side of the
oracle is an independent comparison producer, not a hidden semantic service
used to manufacture Sage's result.
This boundary makes external metadata reusable without masking gaps in Sage's
semantics or creating accidental whole-crate dependencies. Its local contract
is [crates.sage_ir.metadata.provider_authority](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/metadata/provider_authority.html); exact oracle
independence remains [Oracle test harness](#oracle-test-harness).
## Semantic evidence starts from source
When a semantic behavior can be produced by a Rust program, integration and
acceptance evidence starts from a checked-in Cargo project and traverses the
production layers named by the claim. A checked-in inline fixture may define
that project through source strings and explicit options, materialized into
an isolated Cargo project with deterministic configuration. Its expected
observations remain outputs; they cannot supply semantic facts to compilation.
The draft [inline compilation test RFD](../inline-compile-tests/README.md)
proposes this authoring form.
Snapshots, query traces, and rendered
review packets are observations of that execution. They are never loaded as
precomputed semantic answers which replace parsing, expansion, resolution,
checking, inspection, or transport.
Constructed values remain useful for focused unit tests, and a narrow test
double may inject an operating-system or external-service failure which cannot
be reproduced safely or deterministically. Such a test establishes only that
boundary. It cannot establish a Sage semantic anchor, and a transport test
over a scripted semantic provider cannot be presented as end-to-end evidence.
This decision makes the authority of a test visible: Rust projects are inputs,
reviewed snapshots are outputs, and production code performs the semantic
work between them. Its general verification contract is
[crates.sage_inspector.inspection.source_evidence](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_inspector/inspection/source_evidence.html); the Semantic Inspector applies it in
[crates.sage_inspector.inspection.source_evidence](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_inspector/inspection/source_evidence.html).
## Overloadable operators remain trait calls through Typed IR
Every successfully proven overloadable operator is represented in completed
Typed IR as a resolved trait-method call, including operations whose current
operands are concrete primitive types. Generic bodies therefore retain the
same semantic representation whether a later instantiation selects a
primitive or user-defined implementation. Non-overloadable lazy boolean
operators remain explicit short-circuit operations.
Primitive recognition belongs after Typed IR. Once generic substitutions are
concrete, future codegen may recognize a supported operator language-item call
and replace it with the corresponding primitive operation; otherwise it uses
ordinary static trait-call lowering. The rustc oracle's fixed projection maps
rustc's earlier scalar classification back into Sage's shared semantic-call
schema, preserving exact independent comparison without making rustc's THIR
representation Sage's architecture.
The body-checking consequence is
[crates.sage_ir.checking.body.operator_calls](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/checking/body/operator_calls.html), the representation invariant is
[crates.sage_ir.types.operators.trait_calls](../../design/anchor/crates/sage_ir/types/operators/trait_calls.html), and the accepted change is specified by
[NIV-A4](../numeric-inference-variables/README.md#niv-a4).
## Architectural pseudocode has checkable dependency envelopes
Compiler architecture is reviewable through `.sage` declarations organized by
crate, symbol, context, and method. Method prose describes intent; structured
envelopes declare permitted calls and forbidden transitive dependencies.
`sage-meta` is the shared build and validation layer connecting Markdown
specifications, `.sage` declarations, and Rust. Its public library validates
model consistency, including known subclass dispatch, Rust correspondence, and
named specification rules' test references. CLI, CI, and workspace Cargo tests
invoke the same check. This separates architectural dependency review from
detailed Rust semantics.
Specification paragraphs use meaningful, stable names with
{anchor}`meta.language.calls.declared` markers. Inert
`#[sage::test(meta.language.calls.declared)]` attributes connect tests to those rules.
Every declared rule has a test and every test reference resolves; source
coverage does not establish execution or assertion quality. Each fine-grained
paragraph states an independently testable rule.
[The Design book is the canonical specification](#the-design-book-is-the-canonical-specification) locates the normative
specification in the Design chapter tree, with equally authoritative Markdown
and `.sage` chapter sources, Rust implementation references, and rule pages.
Rust declares correspondence with inert `#[sage::item(...)]` tool attributes.
Every modeled crate/module, named declaration, and declared method has a
crate-correct source anchor; abstract concepts use explicit module markers.
The browser and checker derive their mappings from that one source index.
A runtime-loaded immutable model checks observed operation entries and query
requests, including cached requests. The same structured evidence supports
conformance diagnostics and planned walkthroughs. Source/build mismatches and
unmapped boundaries remain explicit gaps. Source anchors, model consistency,
and observed conformance are separate claims; none establishes exhaustive Rust
semantics. The living contract and current limitations are in
[Architectural Pseudocode](../../design/meta/language.md).
## The Design book is the canonical specification
The mdBook Design chapter tree is the normative specification. Markdown and
`.sage` are equally authoritative source formats inside the book source
directory, `md/`. `.sage` chapters live in directories identifying their modeled
crates, with `crate.sage` manifests. This gives prose and architectural models
one navigable authority instead of separate corpora whose relationship must
be inferred. Crates content from `design/crates/<crate>/*.sage` follows the
[display specification](../../design/meta/book.md#displaying-sage-files): structured
declarations, search, dependency navigation, Rust source access, and consistent
book, export, and local-server delivery. Every
modeled entity has a direct link usable elsewhere in the book or model. Entity
links use model identities independently of paragraph anchor names; making an
entity linkable does not automatically declare a specification rule.
An anchor's identity combines the full chapter source path relative to Design and
the rule's local name; headings do not affect identity. Moving a chapter renames
its anchors: update references
and redirect old URLs. Moving a model source does not change its compiler model
item identities. A generated hierarchical index exposes anchor text and status;
each anchor also has a page linking its definition, context, implementation,
and tests or recorded evidence.
Every rule has implementation and test entries, with explicit `todo` and
`not_applicable` accounting displayed as **TODO** and **N/A**. The book and
anchor system describe themselves
using the same anchors and coverage requirements, without privileged exemptions.
Declared associations remain distinct from observed results. The shared
`sage-meta` check validates them in CI and workspace tests; plain `cargo build`
need not run it.
RFDs explain a change and its implementation plan on the same branch as the
normative Design changes. They do not hold a competing specification that must
be promoted upon completion. The living contract and current limitations are
in [The Design Book](../../design/meta/book.md); source-reference and coverage details are
in [Architectural Pseudocode](../../design/meta/anchors.md#specification-tests-and-workspace-checks).
# Overview
Sage is a demand-driven Rust semantic frontend. Symbols give definitions stable
identities. Parsing and expansion create those symbols; resolution discovers
them; signature and body queries compute semantic products when requested.
Checking a body brings together name resolution, type inference, trait solving,
and elaboration into a completed typed tree.
```mermaid
flowchart LR
Source[Source] --> Symbols[Parse and expand symbols]
Symbols --> Resolve[Resolve names]
Resolve --> Signature[Check signatures]
Signature --> Body[Check and elaborate a body]
Metadata[Dependency metadata] --> Resolve
Metadata --> Signature
Infer[Inference and trait solving] --> Body
Body --> Typed[Typed IR]
This is a map of demand boundaries, not a mandatory batch sequence. Start with
[Crates](crates/README.md) to follow the modeled entities and operations.
- [Meta](meta/README.md) specifies how this book, its architecture language,
source correspondence, and review system work.
- [Tenets](tenets.md) explains the principles behind the design.
- [Anchors](anchor/README.md) lists the specification's named claims with
generated implementation and test status. Every rule has a page connecting
its source definition, implementation excerpts, tests, and review.
- [Crates](crates/README.md) is a guided entry into the compiler model. Its
subchapters render `.sage` declarations and their Rust implementations.
- [RFDs](../rfds/README.md) record changes, alternatives, rationale, and plans.
Their normative changes are expressed directly in this specification.
Markdown and `.sage` are equally authoritative specification formats. Each
anchor states one independently testable claim. A source badge opens the
anchor's generated page; its context link returns to the definition.
**TODO** and **N/A** describe explicit implementation or test entries, not
successful verification. Evidence and status are generated from code, tests,
and saved reviews rather than maintained as a second specification.
For tool usage, start with the [User's Guide](../guide/README.md).
# Crates
The compiler is organized around symbols: a definition has a stable identity,
and its signature, members, or body are computed when requested. The crate
subchapters expose that architecture as searchable `.sage` declarations,
operations, and dependency envelopes. Open **Rust source** on an entity to
inspect its corresponding implementation.
## Following a compilation
Start with [module parsing and expansion](sage_ir/modules.sage), then follow
[symbols](sage_ir/symbols.sage) to their signature and body operations.
[Checking](sage_ir/checking.sage) introduces the computation-local contexts
that [resolve names](sage_ir/resolution.sage), [infer types](sage_ir/inference.sage),
and [solve trait goals](sage_ir/solver.sage). These are demand boundaries:
requesting one body need not compute every body in a crate.
## Semantic values and storage
[Types and checked results](sage_ir/types.sage) describe the semantic values
passed between operations. The [Stash storage model](sage_stash/storage.sage)
explains how those values are owned. [External metadata](sage_ir/metadata.sage)
supplies facts about dependency definitions.
## Understanding and checking results
The [Semantic Inspector](sage_inspector/crate.sage) exposes compiler products
for exploration. The [oracle harness](sage_oracle_harness/crate.sage) compares
Sage with independently emitted rustc results. Their command-line usage is
covered in the [User's Guide](../../guide/README.md).
The [inline compilation tests](sage_test_harness/compile-tests.md)
keep source fixtures, type and symbol observations, diagnostics, and query expectations
inside ordinary annotated Cargo tests. Its
[RFD](../../rfds/inline-compile-tests/README.md) explains the design.
The [specification tooling](sage_meta/crate.sage) checks the correspondence
between this model, named specification rules, and Rust code and tests.
The [Anchors](../anchor/README.md) chapter gathers those rules and their
implementation and test status. [Worked examples](../examples.md) provide
concrete programs to follow through the compiler.
